subject: English Language
assessment_title: Term 3 Controlled Assessment: Integrated Language and Visual Literacy
blueprint: CAPS-aligned integrated assessment: comprehension, summary, language structures, visual literacy, editing, transactional writing, and response planning.

visual_blueprint.subject: English Language

source_type_reasons: Term/theme content references visual source material.

assessment_content_focus: integrated comprehension, summary and language structures
editing for grammar, diction, register and punctuation
formal transactional writing and controlled response planning
content_alignment_notes: CAPS term/content alignment requires educator confirmation.

required_visuals.title: Text response and language planner
required_visuals.assessment_use: Learners plan reading/viewing and writing responses.

generation_constraints: Plan visual evidence before writing questions.
If a question references a map, graph, table, diagram, source, performance space, or practical setup, the matching visual must be present in required_visuals.
Do not create blank source placeholders unless the task explicitly requires the educator to insert an external source.
Use the visual as assessable evidence: questions must ask learners to read, complete, compare, cite, label, calculate from, or reflect on it.
validation_rules: No learner-facing question may refer to a missing visual.
Every required visual must have a clear assessment role: stimulus, learner workspace, marking evidence, or moderation evidence.
Visuals must match subject, phase, term/content focus, and assessment family.

sections.title: Section A: Comprehension and Summary
sections.instructions: Read the passage below and answer ALL the questions in your own words unless otherwise stated.
sections.stimulus: Passage: 'The Silent Language of Bees' – An adapted article discussing how honeybees communicate through dance, the role of pheromones, and the impact of pesticides on colony health. (Approximately 450 words.)

questions.question: In your own words, explain what the 'waggle dance' communicates to other bees.
memo: The waggle dance communicates the direction and distance of a food source (2).
Accept: It tells other bees where to find nectar/pollen.

questions.question: Why does the author describe the bee colony as a 'superorganism'? Quote TWO separate phrases from the passage to support your answer.
memo: The colony acts as a single unit (1).
Quote 1: e.g., 'each bee works for the good of the hive' (1).
Quote 2: e.g., 'the colony functions as one entity' (1).
Accept any two relevant quotes.

questions.question: Refer to paragraph 3. Explain the cause-and-effect relationship between neonicotinoid pesticides and bee navigation.
memo: Pesticides impair the bee's memory/navigation (cause) (1).
This leads to bees failing to return to the hive (effect) (1).

questions.question: State whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE and quote a phrase from the passage to justify your answer: 'Pheromones are only used for reproduction.'
memo: FALSE (1).
Quote: 'pheromones also signal alarm and mark food sources' (1).

questions.question: What is the author's main purpose in writing this passage? Give a reason for your answer.
memo: To inform/educate readers about bee communication and threats (1).
Reason: The passage provides factual information and raises awareness about pesticide effects (1).

questions.question: Explain the irony in the statement: 'The very chemicals meant to protect crops are now silencing the bees that pollinate them.'
memo: Irony: Pesticides intended to help crops harm the pollinators essential for crop production (2).
Accept: The solution becomes the problem.

questions.question: List SEVEN key points from the passage that could be used in a summary on 'How bees communicate and why they are under threat.' Write your points in full sentences, using your own words.
memo: Bees use the waggle dance to share food locations (1).
Pheromones convey alarm, identity, and food signals (1).
The colony operates as a superorganism (1).
Pesticides impair bee navigation and memory (1).
Habitat loss reduces foraging areas (1).
Climate change disrupts flowering cycles (1).
Bee decline threatens global food security (1).
Accept any 7 clear points from the passage.

sections.title: Section B: Visual Literacy – Cartoon and Advertisement
sections.instructions: Study the cartoon and advertisement provided (not shown here, but described in the questions) and answer the questions that follow.
sections.stimulus: Cartoon: A single-panel cartoon showing a farmer standing in a field, holding a smartphone, with a speech bubble saying 'My bees are on strike!' A bee in the foreground wears a tiny protest sign reading 'No flowers, no work!' Advertisement: A full-colour print ad for 'BeeKind Honey' showing a jar of honey with a bee on the label, and the slogan 'Pure sweetness, no compromise.'

questions.question: Refer to the cartoon. What is the farmer's tone in the speech bubble? Substantiate your answer.
memo: Tone: Frustrated/humorous (1).
Substantiation: The statement 'My bees are on strike!' is an absurd, exaggerated complaint (1).

questions.question: Explain the visual irony in the cartoon.
memo: Irony: The bees are protesting for flowers, but the field appears barren (1).
The farmer expects work from bees without providing the natural resources they need (1).

questions.question: In the advertisement, what does the bee on the label symbolise? Give a reason for your answer.
memo: Symbolises naturalness/purity (1).
Reason: Bees are associated with honey and nature, reinforcing the product's natural appeal (1).

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of the slogan 'Pure sweetness, no compromise' in appealing to the target market.
memo: Effective because it uses alliteration (pure/promise) (1).
It emphasises both quality (sweetness) and ethical purity (no compromise) (1).
It appeals to health-conscious consumers seeking natural products (1).

questions.question: Compare the use of colour in the cartoon and the advertisement. How does colour contribute to the message in each?
memo: Cartoon: likely dull/brown tones to show barrenness (1) – reinforces the lack of flowers (1).
Advertisement: bright yellow/golden tones (1) – evoke warmth and natural sweetness (1).

sections.title: Section C: Language Structures and Editing
sections.instructions: Answer the following questions on language structures and edit the given paragraph.
sections.stimulus: Paragraph for editing: 'The bees was busy collecting nectar from the flowers. Their hive, located in an old oak tree, were a marvel of nature. Each bee have a specific role to play, and they work together harmoniously. The queen bee, which is the mother of all the bees, lay thousands of eggs. Without bees, our food supply will collapse.'

questions.question: Correct the verb agreement error in the first sentence: 'The bees was busy...'
memo: Change 'was' to 'were' (1).

questions.question: Rewrite the second sentence in the present tense: 'Their hive, located in an old oak tree, were a marvel of nature.'
memo: Their hive, located in an old oak tree, is a marvel of nature (2).
Accept: 'is' for 'were'.

questions.question: Identify and correct the subject-verb agreement error in the sentence: 'Each bee have a specific role to play.'
memo: Error: 'have' should be 'has' (1).
Corrected: Each bee has a specific role to play (1).

questions.question: Change the following sentence from active to passive voice: 'The queen bee lays thousands of eggs.'
memo: Thousands of eggs are laid by the queen bee (2).
Accept: 'are laid' for 'lays'.

questions.question: Rewrite the final sentence in the first conditional: 'Without bees, our food supply will collapse.'
memo: If bees disappear, our food supply will collapse (2).
Accept: 'If bees die out, our food supply will collapse.'

questions.question: Provide the correct form of the word in brackets: 'The (important) of bees cannot be overstated.'
memo: importance (1).

questions.question: Combine the following sentences into a single sentence using a relative clause: 'The hive is in the oak tree. The oak tree is centuries old.'
memo: The hive is in the oak tree, which is centuries old (2).
Accept: 'The hive is in the oak tree that is centuries old.'

sections.title: Section D: Transactional Writing and Response Planning
sections.instructions: Choose ONE of the following topics and write a response of 180–200 words. Use the provided planner to structure your response.
sections.stimulus: Topic 1: Write a formal letter to the local municipality expressing concern about the use of pesticides in public parks and requesting a review of the policy. Topic 2: Write a blog post aimed at teenagers, explaining why bees are important and how they can help protect them.

questions.question: Using the 'Text response and language planner' (Figure 1), complete the 'Main idea' and 'Evidence' sections for your chosen topic.
memo: Main idea clearly stated (2).
Evidence includes at least two relevant points from the passage or own knowledge (2).

questions.question: Write your chosen response (formal letter or blog post) in the 'Draft' section of the planner. Ensure your response is well-structured, uses appropriate register, and is 180–200 words long.
memo: Content: 10 marks – relevance, development, and argument.
Structure: 5 marks – logical organisation, paragraphing.
Language: 5 marks – grammar, punctuation, register, and tone.

questions.question: After writing your draft, use the 'Edit' section of the planner to correct at least TWO language or punctuation errors in your response. List the corrections you made.
memo: Identifies two errors (2).
Provides corrected versions (2).
Accept any plausible corrections.

rubric.descriptor: Accurate retrieval, interpretation, and concise summarisation of key points.
Analysis and evaluation of visual texts with reference to specific details.
Correct application of grammar, punctuation, and sentence structure.
Effective planning, drafting, and editing of a formal or informal response.

teacher_review_checklist: Verify that the reading passage is original or appropriately adapted and within copyright limits.
Confirm that the cartoon and advertisement descriptions are clear enough for learners to visualise without actual images.
Check that the summary question requires exactly seven points and that the memo allows equivalent wording.
Ensure the editing paragraph contains the intended errors and that the corrections are unambiguous.
Confirm that the writing topics are appropriate for Grade 12 and that the rubric aligns with CAPS requirements.
Verify that the total marks for all sections sum to 70 and the duration is 2 hours.
